Over the weekend, I had the chance to join some outstanding @HumbleISD JROTC students for a Saturday morning workout. Let me tell you, it’s pretty inspiring to see young men and women choosing to push themselves, to embrace the challenge, and to show up when it’s not easy.

Workouts like this aren’t just about getting stronger—they’re about accountability, teamwork, and learning that the hardest things in life are often the most rewarding. There’s a reason the military focuses on shared suffering—it builds trust, resilience, and bonds that last a lifetime.

Nothing is given. Everything is earned.

This means making President Trump’s price transparency rules for hospitals and insurers law, so that Americans know what they are paying for health care services. Right now, we have little to no knowledge of negotiated prices, making it very difficult to have free market forces. Transparency will create market competition and lower prices.

This also means requiring drug middle men, like pharmacy benefit managers, to report transparent prices and discounts. This is a common sense policy that most Americans support. This information will give employers and patients the ability to shop for better prescription drug benefits that lower drug costs.

Hamas doesn’t fight fair. They hide behind civilians, building tunnels under hospitals, schools, and homes, knowing full well Israel’s rules of engagement will hold them back.

John Spencer (@SpencerGuard), Chair of Urban Warfare Studies at West Point, breaks it down: when armies can’t use precision strikes, wars become longer, bloodier, and deadlier. Just look at Stalingrad, where a single building became a months-long fight. Gaza is no different—this is what happens when terrorists exploit humanity’s moral restraint.

John joined me to cut through the myths about urban combat and explain the realities unfolding in Ukraine, Syria, and Gaza. We also look ahead: what would a Chinese invasion of Taiwan look like? How do we combat cartels on our southern border? These are the hard questions we have to confront if we want to win wars and protect civilians.

Watch this clip. Then check out the full conversation. John Spencer knows his stuff—and tells it like it is.

Grateful for their service, their dedication, and the chance to experience a small piece of what they do every day.
